levels.1.title: Your first diagram
levels.1.intro: Richard Feynman invented a visual language to describe how particles interact. Each line is a particle, and time runs from left to right. Let's learn its first letters.
levels.1.steps.electron.prompt: Straight lines with an arrow represent electrons. Tap one.
levels.1.steps.electron.wrong.int: That line is wavy: it's a photon. Look for a straight one with an arrow.
levels.1.steps.electron.wrongDefault: Look for a straight line with an arrow in the middle.
levels.1.steps.electron.hints.0: There are four straight lines: two on the left and two on the right.
levels.1.steps.electron.hints.1: Any straight line with an arrow will do: they're all electrons.
levels.1.steps.electron.solved: That's it! Straight with an arrow: electron (e⁻).
levels.1.steps.photon.prompt: The wavy line is a photon, the particle of light. Tap it.
levels.1.steps.photon.wrongDefault: That line is straight: it's an electron. The photon is drawn wavy.
levels.1.steps.photon.hints.0: Look for the only line that isn't straight.
levels.1.steps.photon.hints.1: It's in the middle, joining the two points where the lines meet.
levels.1.steps.time.prompt: With the convention we use, which way does time run in the diagram?
levels.1.steps.time.options.lr.feedback: On the left, what comes in; on the right, what goes out.
levels.1.steps.time.options.tb.feedback: Some books use that convention, but here time always flows from left to right (look at the axis at the bottom).
levels.1.steps.time.options.none.feedbac: They do have a time direction: it separates the initial state (left) from the final one (right).
levels.1.steps.time.hints.0: Look at the arrow below the diagram.
levels.1.steps.time.hints.1: The initial particles are drawn on the left.
levels.1.success: You can read your first two “letters”! Straight with an arrow: electron. Wavy: photon.
levels.1.explanation.intuitive: Two electrons approach, exchange a photon and move apart. That's how two negative charges repel each other.
levels.1.explanation.scientific: It's a tree-level electron–electron scattering diagram (Møller scattering). The four external fermion lines are the initial and final electrons; the internal wavy line is a virtual photon.
levels.1.explanation.math: Each element of the diagram contributes a factor to a probability amplitude 𝓜. This diagram has two vertices, so its contribution is proportional to e², where e is the elementary charge.
levels.2.title: In and out
levels.2.intro: Every diagram tells a story: some particles come in (initial state) and others go out (final state). In between, they interact.
levels.2.steps.initial.prompt: Tap all the particles of the initial state (the ones coming in) and press Check.
levels.2.steps.initial.wrong.int: That photon is internal: it starts and ends inside the diagram, so it neither comes in nor goes out.
levels.2.steps.initial.wrongDefault: That line reaches the right edge: it leaves the process.
levels.2.steps.initial.hints.0: The particles coming in are on the left.
levels.2.steps.initial.hints.1: They're the two straight lines touching the left edge.
levels.2.steps.count.prompt: How many particles are there in the final state?
levels.2.steps.count.options.2.feedback: Two electrons leave on the right.
levels.2.steps.count.options.3.feedback: The photon doesn't count: it joins two vertices inside the diagram, so it doesn't go out.
levels.2.steps.count.options.4.feedback: Count only the lines that reach the right edge.
levels.2.steps.count.hints.0: Count the lines that reach the right edge.
levels.2.steps.count.hints.1: The central photon doesn't reach any edge.
levels.2.steps.role.prompt: Two electrons come in and two electrons go out. What role does the photon play?
levels.2.steps.role.options.mediator.tex: It carries the electromagnetic interaction between them
levels.2.steps.role.options.mediator.fee: The photon is the mediator of the electromagnetic force.
levels.2.steps.role.options.third.text: It's a third electron being created
levels.2.steps.role.options.third.feedba: It's wavy: it's a photon, not an electron.
levels.2.steps.role.options.escape.text: It escapes and we could detect it
levels.2.steps.role.options.escape.feedb: A photon joining two vertices is internal (virtual): it never reaches a detector.
levels.2.steps.role.hints.0: The photon joins the two points where something happens.
levels.2.steps.role.hints.1: Think of it as the force's “messenger”.
levels.2.success: You can now tell the beginning from the end of a quantum story.
levels.2.explanation.intuitive: What comes in is on the left; what goes out, on the right. The central photon is the “messenger” of the interaction.
levels.2.explanation.scientific: External lines represent real particles of the initial and final states, the ones prepared and detected in an experiment. Internal lines represent virtual particles, which aren't observed directly.
levels.2.explanation.math: For each initial and final state we compute an amplitude 𝓜. The probability of the process is proportional to |𝓜|².
levels.3.title: The backward arrow
levels.3.intro: Every particle has an antiparticle with the opposite charge. The electron's is the positron (e⁺). It's drawn with the same straight line, but with the arrow pointing against time.
levels.3.steps.positron-in.prompt: Tap the positron coming into the interaction.
levels.3.steps.positron-in.wrong.in1: That one comes in, but its arrow points forward in time: it's an electron.
levels.3.steps.positron-in.wrong.out2: It's a positron, but it's on the right: it goes out. Look for the one coming in.
levels.3.steps.positron-in.wrong.out1: That line goes out and its arrow points forward in time: it's an electron.
levels.3.steps.positron-in.wrongDefault: Look for a line on the left with the arrow pointing left.
levels.3.steps.positron-in.hints.0: Look only at the lines on the left.
levels.3.steps.positron-in.hints.1: The positron's arrow points backward in time, that is, to the left.
levels.3.steps.charge.prompt: What electric charge does a positron have?
levels.3.steps.charge.options.pos.feedba: Same mass as the electron, opposite charge.
levels.3.steps.charge.options.neg.feedba: An antiparticle has the opposite charge to its particle.
levels.3.steps.charge.options.zero.feedb: The positron has charge: that's why it can emit and absorb photons.
levels.3.steps.positron-out.prompt: Now tap the positron going out.
levels.3.steps.positron-out.wrong.out1: It goes out, but with the arrow forward in time: it's an electron.
levels.3.steps.positron-out.wrongDefault: Look on the right for an arrow pointing left.
levels.3.steps.positron-out.hints.1: Its arrow also points left, against time.
levels.3.success: You've discovered antimatter. The same line, with the arrow reversed.
levels.3.explanation.intuitive: An electron and a positron pass each other and are deflected by exchanging a photon.
levels.3.explanation.scientific: It's Bhabha scattering (e⁻e⁺ → e⁻e⁺) in the t channel. The arrow doesn't show where the particle moves, but the flow of fermion number. An arrow against time represents an antiparticle moving into the future.
levels.3.explanation.math: In the amplitude, an incoming electron contributes a spinor u(p) and an incoming positron a spinor v̄(p). The order is still e².
levels.4.title: Name every line
levels.4.intro: You now know the electron, the positron and the photon. With these three pieces you can write all of quantum electrodynamics (QED). Read this new diagram.
levels.4.steps.photons.prompt: Tap all the photons in the diagram and press Check.
levels.4.steps.photons.wrong.int: That line is straight: it's a (virtual) electron, even though it's inside the diagram.
levels.4.steps.photons.wrong.in2: Straight with the arrow pointing backward: it's a positron.
levels.4.steps.photons.wrong.in1: Straight with the arrow pointing forward: it's an electron.
levels.4.steps.photons.hints.1: Both photons are on the right.
levels.4.steps.process.prompt: What process does this diagram represent?
levels.4.steps.process.options.annihilat: An electron and a positron annihilate and produce two photons
Matter and antimatter turn into light.
Two photons collide and create an electron and a positron
Look at the direction of time: the photons are on the right, so they go out.
An electron emits two photons and carries on
The bottom line has its arrow pointing backward: it's a positron, not another electron.
levels.4.steps.process.hints.0: What comes in on the left?
levels.4.steps.process.hints.1: One arrow forward and one backward: an electron and a positron.
levels.4.success: You're reading diagrams you'd never seen before. That's how you learn a language.
levels.4.explanation.intuitive: When an electron meets a positron, they can disappear and turn into light: two photons.
levels.4.explanation.scientific: It's the annihilation of an electron–positron pair into two photons (e⁻e⁺ → γγ). The internal line is a virtual electron joining the two vertices. It's used, for example, in positron emission tomography (PET).
levels.4.explanation.math: Again there are two vertices, so the amplitude is of order e². There's another diagram with the photons swapped, and it's added to this one to get the total amplitude.
levels.5.title: Not a photograph
levels.5.intro: Feynman's language is very precise: a wrong label changes the meaning. This diagram has a notation mistake. Can you find it?
levels.5.steps.label.prompt: One label doesn't match what the drawing says. Tap the mislabelled line.
levels.5.steps.label.wrongDefault: That line's label matches its drawing. Check which way each arrow points.
levels.5.steps.label.hints.0: Compare each arrow with the direction of time.
levels.5.steps.label.hints.1: A line with the arrow pointing backward should be called e⁺.
levels.5.steps.label.solved: Backward arrow coming in: it's a positron, not an electron.
levels.5.steps.trajectory.prompt: A friend says: “The top electron travels exactly along that path and bounces off the photon.” What would you tell her?
levels.5.steps.trajectory.options.amplit: The diagram isn't a trajectory: it represents a contribution to the probability of the process
Exactly. The positions and angles in the drawing mean nothing: all that matters is what's connected to what.
levels.5.steps.trajectory.options.yes.te: She's right: the lines are the real paths
levels.5.steps.trajectory.options.yes.fe: Quantum particles don't follow definite paths like balls. If we draw the diagram differently, it means the same thing.
levels.5.steps.trajectory.options.curved: Almost: the real path is curved
Neither straight nor curved: the diagram doesn't describe any path in space.
levels.5.steps.trajectory.hints.0: Would the physics change if we drew the lines longer or tilted?
levels.5.steps.trajectory.hints.1: A Feynman diagram is a piece of a calculation of probability amplitudes.
levels.5.success: You found the mistake and avoided the most common misconception about Feynman diagrams.
levels.5.explanation.intuitive: A Feynman diagram is like a subway map: it tells you what's connected to what, not exactly where things go.
levels.5.explanation.scientific: A Feynman diagram represents a contribution to the probability amplitude of a process. It's not a photograph of trajectories: the positions of vertices and lines on paper have no physical meaning, only the topology and the line types.
levels.5.explanation.math: Each vertex of the diagram is integrated over every position in spacetime. That's why the drawing doesn't fix any particular trajectory.
